t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle distinguishes three questions. Which one does the paper actually address?
a: Is the brain a digital computer?
w: Is the mind a computer program?
Can brain operations be simulated on a computer?
e: He says 'Is the mind a program?' is decisively NO (Chinese Room). 'Can the brain be simulated?' is trivially YES (Church's thesis).

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Match Searle's labels: 'the mind is a program' / 'brain processes can be simulated' / 'the brain is a digital computer'.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle's 'Primal Story' behind Cognitivism rests on which two results in mathematical logic?
w: Bayes' theorem and the halting problem
e: The Church-Turing thesis and Turing's theorem (a Universal Turing Machine can simulate any TM). Suppose the brain is a Universal Turing Machine... That idea 'sent shivers down the spines' of a generation.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: In the Primal Story, why is semantics supposed to 'take care of itself'?
w: The brain has no semantics at all
e: Proof theory shows semantic relations can be mirrored by purely syntactic relations. So if we account for syntactic processes, semantics follows. Searle disputes this.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Block's example of a computer built from cats, mice and cheese illustrates the cognitivists' delight in:
e: Multiple realizability: computations can be realized in almost any physical medium. Searle says this 'delight' is a symptom of something going wrong.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Why does Searle say multiple realizability of computation differs from that of carburetors?
a: Computation is defined by assigned syntax, not physics
w: Carburetors can't actually be multiply realized at all
Computation needs silicon chips in order to be realized
There is no real difference between the two cases
e: Carburetors are defined by physical effects; computation is defined purely by assigning syntax. So the same principle implies universal realizability: anything could be described as a digital computer.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle's 'wall behind me' example claims that:
a: Some pattern in it implements a word processor
w: Walls can think if they are large enough
Walls block the signals computers need
Only walls, not brains, are computers
e: For a big enough wall, some pattern of molecular movements is isomorphic with the Wordstar program. On the textbook definition, almost everything is implementing some program.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle's central new claim (beyond the Chinese Room) is that:
w: Physics is itself a computer program
e: Syntax is not intrinsic to physics; it's observer-relative. Ten years ago: syntax isn't sufficient for semantics. Now: syntax isn't even intrinsic to physics.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle compares discovering a computer in nature to discovering:
e: Chairs: we can find objects shaped like chairs, but they only 'function as chairs' relative to users. Similarly, you can't discover sentences in the head, since something is a sentence only relative to an agent using it as one.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle says cognitive science escapes the observer-relativity problem only by committing the:
e: Homunculus fallacy: treating the brain as if some agent inside uses it to compute. E.g., Marr's vision theory outputs a '3-D description'. Who is reading it?

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Why does Searle think Dennett's 'discharging the homunculus' via recursive decomposition fails?
a: Even the bottom level's syntax is observer-assigned
w: There are infinitely many levels to go through
The flip-flops at the bottom are conscious
e: Even at the bottom (flip-flops reading '0' or '1'), syntax is still assigned by an outside homunculus. Decomposition addresses a different question. Without an outside observer, there is no syntax even at the bottom.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle points out a common arithmetic error: 6 × 8 is 6 added to itself how many times?
e: Six added to itself eight times would be 54. 'It is amazing how often this mistake is made.'

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle's third difficulty is that syntax has no:
e: 0's and 1's as such exist only in the eye of the beholder. The program has no causal powers beyond the implementing medium.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle's frog 'bug detector' example (Lettvin et al.) shows that:
a: Once we know the biology, no one calls it a program
w: Frogs really do run something like computer programs
Frogs can't actually see the moving bugs they catch
Neurobiology turns out to be irrelevant to vision
e: Once we know how a system works neurobiologically, nobody calls it 'mere hardware implementation' of a program. Likewise, a word processor simulating a typewriter doesn't explain how typewriters work.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Unlike the mechanical computer, the human doing long division in Turing's contrast:
w: Has no program level at all
e: Is consciously following rules, so there really is a causal program level. In the brain there's no such intrinsic rule-following, and no homunculus to interpret it.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle's fourth difficulty is that the brain does not:
w: Respond to light hitting the eye
e: Do information processing in the sense computers do. In computers, an outside agent encodes and interprets the information. In the brain, specific electro-chemical processes cause concrete conscious experiences.

t: Searle – Is the Brain a Digital Computer?
q: Searle concludes that 'The brain is a digital computer' is:
a: Too unclear to even be false
e: Not false, but lacking a clear enough sense to be false: like 'Is it an abacus?'. You could assign a computational interpretation to the brain just as to anything else.
